register.name: Medical emergency
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Far from emergency care
sub_causes.note: Ambulances take about twice as long to reach rural homes (a median of about 14 minutes against 7).

sub_causes.name: Falls
sub_causes.note: Falls are a leading reason older adults need emergency care; clear floors and light the way at night.

register.name: Hurricane
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (88–98) will lose power or have damage from a hurricane or tropical storm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Inland flooding from a tropical storm
sub_causes.note: A weakening hurricane can drop a foot or more of rain far inland (Helene in western North Carolina, 2024), cutting water service for weeks.

register.name: Phone or internet outage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (63 to nearly all) will lose phone and internet service for hours in a network outage in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: GPS or radio disruption
sub_causes.note: Space weather or jamming can degrade navigation and timing. Keep a paper map for the way home.

register.name: Supply chain disruption
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 86 (63–98) will find store shelves empty of things they need in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Fuel shortage
sub_causes.note: Gas stations run dry for days (the Colonial Pipeline shutdown, May 2021, and before hurricanes). It matters most with a generator or a long drive.

sub_causes.name: Cut off: an island or a single road
sub_causes.note: A bridge, ferry or the only road closes and the community is cut off for days. Plan for longer if that is you.

register.name: Local water or gas outage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 78 (50–95) will have a water main break or boil-water notice in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Toxic algae in the water supply
sub_causes.note: Algae toxins reach the treatment plant and a do-not-drink order follows (Toledo, 2014). Counted in the water-notice rate.

sub_causes.name: Gas main over-pressure or leak
sub_causes.note: Gas mains over-pressure or leak and homes must be evacuated (Merrimack Valley, 2018). If you smell gas, leave first, then call.

sub_causes.name: Water system failure for weeks
sub_causes.note: A treatment plant or system fails for weeks (Jackson, Mississippi, 2022; Asheville, 2024). The water targets use the county's drinking-water violations to size it.

sub_causes.name: Sewer failure
sub_causes.note: Pumps stop or mains break and toilets cannot be flushed. The sanitation supplies follow the water target.

register.name: Stranded in a vehicle
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 78 (39–98) will be stranded away from home by a crash, breakdown or shutdown in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Black ice or dense fog
sub_causes.note: Chain-reaction crashes and closed highways. Counted in the stranding rate.

sub_causes.name: Transit shutdown or strike
sub_causes.note: Buses and trains stop and commuters without a car are stuck. Counted for commuters who travel by transit.

register.name: Job loss
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 71 (52–89) will have someone lose a job in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Livestock or poultry disease
sub_causes.note: An animal-disease outbreak (bird flu in dairy or poultry) can hit a farm's income.

sub_causes.name: Recession layoffs
sub_causes.note: Layoffs cluster in downturns; the high end of the job-loss range is a recession year.

register.name: Medicine shortage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 53 (25–90) will have a daily medicine they cannot fill for days or weeks because of a shortage in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Hospital supply shock
sub_causes.note: A key hospital supply runs short (IV fluids in 2024, after Hurricane Helene closed a plant that makes a large share of the country's supply) and planned care is delayed.

register.name: Heat wave
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 29 (16–45) will go through a heat wave in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A blackout during a heat wave
sub_causes.note: When the power fails in extreme heat, air conditioning fails for everyone at once. It is the most dangerous combination; where it matters most it is a named scenario.

register.name: Civil unrest
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 26 (10–45) will live under a curfew because of unrest in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Unrest around elections
sub_causes.note: Protests, clashes or curfews around elections or political events.

register.name: Chemical spill or release
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 19 (7–41) will be told not to drink the tap water, or to stay inside, after a chemical spill in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Release from a chemical plant
sub_causes.note: A plant that uses large amounts of toxic or flammable chemicals has a release or explosion (West, Texas, 2013). Counted in the chemical-release rate.

sub_causes.name: Train derailment with chemicals
sub_causes.note: A train carrying chemicals derails and burns or leaks; homes within a mile or two are evacuated (East Palestine, 2023).

sub_causes.name: Tanker truck spill
sub_causes.note: A tanker crash closes roads and may bring an order to stay inside nearby.

sub_causes.name: Pipeline rupture
sub_causes.note: A gas or oil transmission pipeline ruptures and burns or spills; nearby homes are evacuated.

sub_causes.name: Refinery, tank farm or port fire
sub_causes.note: A large industrial fire brings orders to stay inside and smoke for days.

sub_causes.name: Chemical spill into the water supply
sub_causes.note: A spill upstream of a water intake brings a do-not-use order for days (Elk River, West Virginia, 2014). Counted in the chemical-release rate.

register.name: Long illness in the household
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 18 (10–45) will have someone sick at home for weeks in the next ten years.

register.name: Cyberattack on services
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 18 (7–39) will lose pharmacy, payment or other services to a computer outage or cyberattack in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Critical software failure
sub_causes.note: A faulty update or cloud outage takes down hospital, airline, bank or 911 systems for a day or more (July 2024). Counted in this rate.

sub_causes.name: Card or bank payment outage
sub_causes.note: Cards, bank apps or cash machines stop for hours to days. Keep some cash in small bills.

register.name: A household member is arrested or detained
register.frequency_sentence: For households with people the ages of yours, about 2 in 100 have someone arrested in a year, going by what people tell a national survey (2022–2024); police records suggest up to about 4 in 100. People arrested once are often arrested again, so over ten years fewer households are affected than a year-by-year count suggests. This counts arrests, not guilt or convictions.

register.name: Burst pipe or water leak
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 14 will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Sewer backup
sub_causes.note: Sewage backs up through basement drains; standard home policies leave it out unless you add sewer-backup cover.

register.name: Strong wind
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 14 (4–43) will lose power or have damage in a windstorm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Derecho
sub_causes.note: A fast line of storms with hurricane-force gusts over hundreds of miles; outages can last days. Counted in the windstorm rate.

register.name: Pandemic
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 11 (3–23) will live through a pandemic that changes daily life in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Mosquito- or tick-borne outbreak
sub_causes.note: Local dengue or West Nile spread brings spraying and advisories.

sub_causes.name: Local disease outbreak
sub_causes.note: Measles, hepatitis A or Legionnaires' in the community keeps people out of school or work. Check your vaccinations.

sub_causes.name: Bird flu (H5N1)
sub_causes.note: A candidate pandemic strain that so far passes from animals to people, not between people.

register.name: Break-in
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 10 (5–18) will have a break-in in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Identity theft and disaster scams
sub_causes.note: Accounts opened in your name, or fake contractors and FEMA impostors after a disaster. A credit freeze is free.

register.name: Earthquake
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 9 will feel an earthquake strong enough to knock things off shelves in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Liquefaction
sub_causes.note: Wet, sandy ground turns to slurry in strong shaking; pipes and foundations fail. Water outages last longer where it happens.

sub_causes.name: Fire after an earthquake
sub_causes.note: Broken gas lines and low water pressure let fires spread after a big earthquake. Know how to shut off the gas, and leave it to the gas company to turn it back on.

register.name: Death or disability of an earner
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 9 (5–14) will lose an earner's income to death or disability in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Death in the family
sub_causes.note: A family member who does not earn dies: funeral costs and time off work.

register.name: House fire
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (3–8) will have a house fire, in their home or next door in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
sub_causes.note: Carbon monoxide from a furnace, generator or car builds up indoors, most often after storms when generators run too close to the house. Shown beside fires, not added to them; a CO alarm is the defence.

sub_causes.name: Lithium battery fire
sub_causes.note: E-bike, scooter and power-bank batteries can catch fire while charging; charge them where you can see them.

register.name: Volcanic eruption
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (2–11) will have ash or mudflows from a volcano reach them in the next ten years.

register.name: Regional blackout
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (1–14) will lose power in a regional blackout that is not caused by weather in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Attack on power substations
sub_causes.note: Gunfire or sabotage at substations can cut power to a county for days (Moore County, North Carolina, 2022). Utilities report about 78 cases of attack, vandalism or theft a year, most with no outage (2019–2023).

sub_causes.name: Cyberattack on the grid
sub_causes.note: Hackers switched off parts of Ukraine's grid in 2015; no US case has cut power. Utilities report about 7 cyber events a year (2019–2023).

register.name: Lightning
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 3 (1–9) will have lightning damage their home or cut their power in the next ten years.

register.name: Flooding from rivers or heavy rain
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (1–7) will be cut off or lose building services in a flood in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Flash flood
sub_causes.note: Water rises in minutes on roads and near creeks; most flood deaths are people driving into it. Counted in the flood rate; turn around, don't drown.

sub_causes.name: Basement or street flooding in heavy rain
sub_causes.note: Drains overflow and water or sewage comes up into basements outside the mapped flood zone. It is the outside-the-zone part of the flood rate, higher with a basement.

sub_causes.name: Levee failure or overtopping
sub_causes.note: Counted on the dam and levee card, not here: leveed land is mapped outside the high-risk flood zone.

register.name: Landslide
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (1–10) will have a landslide cut off their road or damage their home in the next ten years. About 2 (1–7) in 1,000 will have one damage their home.

register.name: Tsunami
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 1 (fewer than 1 to 2) will have to leave home or work for a tsunami warning in the next ten years.

register.name: Coastal flooding
register.frequency_sentence: About 9 (4–28) in 1,000 households like yours will be cut off or lose building services in coastal flooding in the next ten years.

register.name: Drought
register.frequency_sentence: About 5 (1–25) in 1,000 households like yours will face water limits in a drought in the next ten years.

register.name: Tornado
register.frequency_sentence: About 1 in 2,400 (1 in 8,300 to 1 in 720) households like yours will have a tornado damage or cut off their neighborhood in the next ten years.

register.name: Power out for months (any cause)
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 15 and 1 in 4 households like yours would be without power for two months or more in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A severe solar storm
sub_causes.note: Long outages where large transformers fail; most places would be back within days.

sub_causes.name: EMP from a nuclear attack
sub_causes.note: Only as part of a nuclear attack; EPRI's 2019 study did not support a nationwide blackout lasting months.

sub_causes.name: Attacks on the grid in a war
sub_causes.note: Cyberattacks, sabotage or missiles on power plants and lines.

sub_causes.name: Your county's own outage record
sub_causes.note: Storms and failures like the ones in your county's outage records, with the long tail the records cannot show yet.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a curfew (about 26 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: No power for months: water, heat, medicine and money all affected. Puerto Rico waited 328 days after Hurricane Maria.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing to stockpile for months. What helps instead: a way to treat water from a nearby source, a way to cook without power, a plan for toilets and waste, and some cash.

register.name: War with attacks on US infrastructure
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 250 and 1 in 13 households like yours would lose power, water or phone service for days to attacks in a war in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: Your county has military sites, a big city, a port or a refinery nearby: the kinds of places attacks on infrastructure aim at.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than the death or disability of an earner (about 9 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Outages of power, water or phones for days, and shortages across the country.

register.name: Financial crisis with bank closures
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 11 households like yours would have banks close for three days or more in a financial crisis in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Your own bank fails
sub_causes.note: Insured deposits (up to $250,000 per person at each bank) move to another bank, usually within days. The FDIC counts about 23 failures a year (2001–2025), most of them small banks.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a pandemic that changes daily life (about 11 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Cards and bank transfers stop for days.
register.what_it_changes: Keep some cash in small bills (already in your plan) and a second account at another bank (free).

register.name: Very large volcanic eruption
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 130 and 1 in 26 households like yours would live through a year or two of higher food prices after a very large eruption somewhere in the world in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A Yellowstone super-eruption
sub_causes.note: Devastation nearby and ash across much of the country. The USGS puts it at about 1 in 730,000 a year.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a regional blackout (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: A year or two of higher food prices and some shortages.

register.name: Severe pandemic
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 21 households like yours would live through a pandemic far deadlier than COVID-19 in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A natural pandemic as deadly as 1918
sub_causes.note: The 1918 flu killed about 675,000 Americans. Records of pandemics over four centuries give the chance.

sub_causes.name: An engineered germ
sub_causes.note: A germ made or changed on purpose. There is no record to count; it is part of the expert range.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than ash or mudflows from a volcano (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Months of disruption, strained hospitals and lost income.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing new: the pandemic row already sizes your food and medicine.

register.name: Nuclear attack or EMP
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 10,000 and 1 in 42 households like yours would be in a blast zone or under dangerous fallout in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Limited strike on US territory
sub_causes.note: One or a few weapons on US soil, for example a strike on Guam, Hawaii, Alaska or a West Coast base. It adds to your chance only where your county is a plausible target.

sub_causes.name: A crude nuclear device in a city
sub_causes.note: Heavy damage within about a mile, and everyone within 50 miles told to get inside. It adds to your chance by your metro area's share of FEMA's terrorism-preparedness money.

sub_causes.name: Electromagnetic pulse (EMP) from a high-altitude burst
sub_causes.note: Only as part of a nuclear attack: a burst high above the lower 48 states could black out a region there; where you live the effect depends on where the burst is. EPRI's 2019 study did not support a nationwide blackout lasting months.

sub_causes.name: Disruption across the country
sub_causes.note: Shortages, power cuts and lost income even far from any target. Shown for everyone and never added to your local chance.

sub_causes.name: A nuclear weapon used elsewhere in the world
sub_causes.note: At home: market shocks, shortages and worry, with no fallout of concern. Never added to your local chance.

location_factor.label: You live in the San Juan metro area: a metro area of more than a million people. Places like this could be targets in a large nuclear war, but they are less likely targets than the biggest cities and military sites.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than lightning damaging your home (about 3 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Serious disruption: sheltering inside for a day or more against fallout, then shortages and outages.
register.what_it_changes: One free step: pick your shelter spot at home and at work (a basement, or the middle of the building away from windows).

register.name: Severe solar storm
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 7,600 and 1 in 150 households like yours would lose power for days to a severe solar storm in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: Your county is at a low geomagnetic latitude (about 28°). Solar storms drive the strongest currents into long power lines nearer the magnetic pole, so the chance of a long outage here is about 0.44 of the national average. The ground's conductivity also matters and is not counted.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than coastal flooding reaching your home (about 9 in 1,000 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Power out for days, and longer where large transformers fail.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing beyond your power plan: a solar storm harms long power lines, not phones or radios.

register.name: Mass shooting or bombing
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 500,000 and 1 in 50,000 households like yours would have someone hurt in a mass shooting or bombing in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: The data are too sparse to say where this is more likely, so the chance is the same everywhere.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a tornado (about 1 in 2,400 for you in the next ten years).
register.what_it_changes: Nothing to buy. Two free steps: know "run, hide, fight", and learn to stop bleeding.

register.name: Chemical, biological or radiological attack
register.frequency_sentence: At most about 1 in 50,000 households like yours would be told to stay inside, or to collect medicine at a public site, after a chemical, biological or radiological attack in the next ten years, and perhaps fewer than 1 in 1,000,000.

sub_causes.name: Chemical
sub_causes.note: A toxic chemical released on purpose: shelter inside for hours, or leave the immediate area if told to.

sub_causes.name: Biological
sub_causes.note: A germ spread on purpose (the anthrax letters of 2001): stay home, and collect preventive medicine at a public site if told to.

sub_causes.name: Radiological ("dirty bomb")
sub_causes.note: Shelter inside for hours; the area may stay closed for weeks.

location_factor.label: San Juan County is outside the 44 urban areas FEMA funds for terrorism preparedness, so an attack that closes your area is much less likely than in the big cities.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a tornado (about 1 in 2,400 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: An order to stay inside for hours, closed buildings, or medicine handed out at public sites.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing beyond your basics: your three-day supplies cover sheltering inside.

buckets.name: No grid power at home
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, nearly all (95 or more) will lose grid power for a day or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 3 months leaves about 10 (4–15) of 100 households like yours facing a longer power cut in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how likely a direct hit by a major hurricane is (expert estimate) and how long the power stays out after a storm like the historic one here (from records).
Power cuts from storms here use your county's outage records since 2014, blended with about 77 nearby counties', because about eleven years is too short to see the rare storms.

The worst power cut in the territory's records was Hurricane Maria (2017); being ready for 3 months would have left some homes that lost power still waiting (about 80 in 100 of all customers there were still out).

buckets.name: Tap water must be treated
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, nearly all (85 or more) will have to boil or treat their tap water for a day or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 6 weeks leaves about 8 (3–25) of 100 households like yours facing a longer boil-water notice in the next 10 years.

This number mostly depends on how long boil-water notices from hurricanes and tropical storms last (expert estimate) and how long boil-water notices from a major water system failure last (expert estimate).

Water-system failures are counted about 9 times as often as the national average here (an expert estimate), because nearly all public-water customers in your county are served by a system with a health-based violation in the last five years (EPA) and you said your water system has frequent notices or outages.
Your gas stove can boil water during a boil-water notice, as long as the gas stays on.

buckets.name: No tap water at all
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 80 (60–95) will have no usable tap water for a day or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 6 months leaves about 2 (0–4) of 100 households like yours facing a longer water outage in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how likely a direct hit by a major hurricane is (expert estimate) and how often a direct hit by a major hurricane stop the tap water (expert estimate).
Public water systems keep pumping on backup power for about 3 days; in longer power cuts some lose pressure, more often where the system has a record of problems.

Water-system failures are counted about 9 times as often as the national average here (an expert estimate), because nearly all public-water customers in your county are served by a system with a health-based violation in the last five years (EPA) and you said your water system has frequent notices or outages.
This rounds up to 6 months: before rounding it is about 3 months, just past 3 months.
The worst loss of tap water on record in your state was in Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria (2017): 2 months for most, up to 5 months. Being ready for 6 months would have covered that.

buckets.name: Can't get to a store
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 65 (40–90) will be unable to shop for food and supplies for 3 days or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 2 weeks leaves about 8 (5–20) of 100 households like yours facing a longer stretch without shopping in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how often pandemics happen where you live (expert estimate) and how long times without shopping from a direct hit by a major hurricane last (expert estimate).

buckets.name: Dangerous heat or cold indoors
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 70 (60–85) will face dangerous heat or cold at home with no working cooling or heating for a day or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 2 weeks leaves about 10 (6–15) of 100 households like yours facing a longer spell of dangerous heat or cold in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how likely a direct hit by a major hurricane is (expert estimate) and how long power cuts from hurricanes and tropical storms last (from records).
A power cut during a heat wave also stops your air conditioning.

buckets.name: Medication and medical-supply continuity
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 80 (75–95) will have trouble getting medicine for 3 days or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 6 months leaves about 2 (0–5) of 100 households like yours facing a longer gap in medicine in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how likely a direct hit by a major hurricane is (expert estimate).
Medicine that must stay cold is at risk in any power cut longer than about a day, unless you have a cooler plan.
This rounds up to 6 months: before rounding it is about 3 months, just past 3 months.

buckets.name: No phone, internet or card payments
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 45 (30–80) will lose phone, internet or card payments for a day or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 5 days leaves about 5 (3–15) of 100 households like yours facing a longer outage in the next 10 years.

This number mostly depends on how long phone and payment outages from a direct hit by a major hurricane last (expert estimate) and how long phone and payment outages from phone or internet network outages last (expert estimate).
This rounds up to 5 days: before rounding it is about 3.4 days, just past 3 days.

buckets.name: Must leave home quickly
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 45 (40–60) will have to leave home quickly at least once in the next 10 years.
Warning can be as short as no warning at all (an earthquake) or as long as 3 days.
For chemical spills and releases, plan for as little as a few minutes of warning; for tsunamis, 15 minutes.
Plan to be away for about 5 days.
Most evacuations last a few days, but after a home fire you could be away for 2 months or more.

buckets.name: Stranded away from home
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 80 (45–100) will have someone stranded away from home at least once in the next 10 years.
The 5-mile (8 km) trip is about an hour and a half on foot; carry about a litre of water for it in hot weather.
The get-home bag is sized by the walk home at about 3 miles an hour, with about half a litre of water per hour in hot weather.

buckets.name: Medical emergency when help is slow
frequency_sentences: Households like yours average about 1 emergency-room visit a year (national figures).

buckets.name: House fire
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (3–8) will have a home fire at least once in the next 10 years.

buckets.name: Home and personal security
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 35 (15–50) will have a break-in or a nearby curfew at least once in the next 10 years.

buckets.name: Unhealthy air indoors
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 10 (5–25) will need to keep smoke, dust or fumes out of the home at least once in the next 10 years.
What helps: a room you can seal, an air cleaner or a box-fan filter, and well-fitting respirators for going outside.

buckets.name: Loss of income
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 20 (10–35) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years.
Aim for about 7 months of income in savings over time, a goal separate from the supplies budget.
This number mostly depends on how long income gaps from losing a job last (expert estimate) and how often job losses happen where you live (expert estimate).
The death or long-term disability of an earner is a question for life and disability insurance, not savings.

buckets.name: Home damaged or uninhabitable
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 15 (10–20) will have to leave home for a while because of damage at least once in the next 10 years.
After a disaster, most displaced households are back within a month, but about 1 in 10 homeowners never return, so insurance and copies of documents matter more than supplies here.

If damage forced you out, 9 in 10 households like yours would be home again within about 9 months; living elsewhere that long costs about $5,200 at 30% of your monthly spending, which loss-of-use insurance pays for.

scenarios.name: Tsunami from a nearby earthquake
scenarios.applies_because: Part of San Juan County is in the tsunami zone: about 6 in 100 residents live there. After a nearby earthquake the first waves can arrive within minutes, so anyone who lives, works or goes to school in the zone should walk to high ground as soon as the shaking stops. Knowing the route costs nothing, so the plan includes it.
scenarios.effect_summary: Does not change your targets at this setting.

scenarios.name: Direct hit by a major hurricane
scenarios.applies_because: Tropical storms and hurricanes reach San Juan County about once every 6 years, and about 1 in 7 of them is a major storm (Category 3 or stronger) that can cut power and water for weeks. Hurricane guidance in Puerto Rico covers it, so the plan includes it.

requirements.plain: 2 battery lights: a headlamp or lantern for each person aged 4 and over. Use lights, not candles. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

2 packs of AA or AAA batteries for the lights and the radio: one pack lasts a household about 7 days. Check which sizes your lights use. Your power target is 90 days; batteries are counted for the first 14 days, and after that a way to recharge (see that line) and rechargeable lights do more than a pile of batteries. (Ready.gov, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

A way to recharge from the car, because your power target of 90 days is longer than the 14 days of batteries and phone power the plan stores: a 12-volt charger, or a small inverter (about 150 W) for chargers that plug into the wall. It tops up phones, power banks, rechargeable lights and a power station. Run the engine only outdoors, never in a garage, even with the door open (CDC). (Oregon OEM, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

1 pair of appliance thermometers, one in the fridge and one in the freezer: after a power cut, keep refrigerated food only if it stayed at 40 °F or below, and throw out perishable food that was above 40 °F for 2 hours or more. (Ready.gov)

1 battery power station (about 1,070 Wh each) to keep refrigerated medicine cool through a 90-day power cut, because a cooler bag lasts only about 1 day. Your essential load (phones) is about 30 Wh a day, 2,700 Wh for 90 days; one station gives about 910 Wh after losses, enough for about 30.3 days of that load. A full-size fridge alone would drain one in about 0.9 days. It can run a small 12-volt cooler for the medicine, or the fridge in short spells. Recharge it from a car, gas or electric, with the engine running outdoors only, or from a solar panel. (retail prices, ENERGY STAR, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Optional for a 90-day outage: a portable solar panel with a battery. In December a 100 W panel near your latitude makes about 382 Wh a day (like Miami, FL (Phoenix, AZ makes 424)). Your essential load of about 30 Wh a day needs about 10 W of panels in full sun; a full-size fridge would need about 260 W. Panels laid flat or in shade make less. (NREL PVWatts, ENERGY STAR; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: keeping a fridge running takes about 995 Wh a day (a chest freezer about 597) × 90 days = 89,550 Wh. A closed fridge keeps food cold about 4 hours and a full freezer about 48; shelf-stable food avoids the need. (ENERGY STAR, Ready.gov)

For a boil-water notice of up to 45 days: make about 1.8 gallons of drinking water safe each day, about 81.6 gallons in all. To make it safe, boil it for 1 minute (3 minutes above 5,000 feet), or add 8 drops of 6 % unscented bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25 %) and wait 30 minutes; double the bleach for cloudy or very cold water. A gas stove can boil water while the gas flows; never use a camp stove or grill indoors. (Ready.gov, PetMD, CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

1 bottle of plain unscented bleach (5 to 9 % sodium hypochlorite, not the splashless kind), for making water safe and for cleaning, however long your target is. At about 0.5 mL a gallon, each ounce treats about 60 gallons of clear water (30 if it is cloudy or very cold), so one bottle treats thousands of gallons. Bleach weakens in storage: buy a fresh bottle every 6 months, when you replace the water you store yourself. (CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

If you boil on a camp stove outdoors, about 11.2 lb of propane brings 309 L to a boil (about 25 to 30 L a pound). Never use a camp stove indoors, and keep no more than 2 one-pound cylinders inside. (EIA, local fire code, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

2 people × 1 gallon a day × 14 days = 28 gallons, plus 4.4 gallons for the dog: about 32.4 gallons. Replace water you store yourself every 6 months. Your target is 180 days. Storing all of it would take about 416.3 gallons, so the plan stores the first 14 days and makes the rest safe with a filter and a water source (see the next line). (Ready.gov, CDC, PetMD, BYU; some amounts are estimates)

Free first step: fill clean drink bottles you already have with tap water, about 6 gallons, the most a household can usually gather this way. Not milk jugs: they leak. Label them and replace the water every 6 months. (Ready Reckoner research, CDC, Ready.gov, Church of Jesus Christ; some amounts are estimates)

After day 14, for the other 166 days: make about 2.3 gallons of water safe each day, about 383.9 gallons in all, with a water filter and rain from your rain barrel, instead of storing more. Filter it, then boil it for 1 minute (3 minutes above 5,000 feet), or add 8 drops of 6 % unscented bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25 %) and wait 30 minutes; double the bleach for cloudy or very cold water. (Ready.gov, CDC, PetMD, BYU; some amounts are estimates)

2 water carriers of about 5 gallons each for hauling water from a distribution point, a neighbour's well or a spring, because your target of 180 days runs past the 14 days of water you store, and the rest has to come from somewhere. A full one weighs about 42 pounds, so choose a size you can carry, with a good handle. (retail prices, EPA; some amounts are estimates)
A two-bucket toilet for when toilets can't flush: 2 sturdy buckets with a seat, one for pee and one for poo. (RDPO, Oregon OEM)

Toilet bags: about 0.45 heavy garbage bags a person a day (0.3 to 0.6), counting both bags of a double-bagged load: 2 people × 30 days = 27 bags. Fill halfway, tie, double-bag, and store away from food, water, children and pets. Don't put them in curbside trash or bury them unless officials say so. Bags are counted for the first 30 days of your 180-day target: if the sewer or septic system still works, it is a better toilet than bags, and officials will say when it is safe to flush. No agency sets a one-month amount: this step sits between the two-week advice (Red Cross, Oregon, Washington) and the Church's three-month pantry. (RDPO, Oregon OEM, EPA, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)

Cover material for the poo bucket (sawdust, shredded paper, dry leaves or pet bedding): about 1 cup a person a day (0.5 to 1.5) × 2 people × 30 days = 60 cups, about 3.8 gallons. (RDPO; some amounts are estimates)

3 household kits of paper plates, cups and utensils, garbage bags with ties, and waterproof matches, one for every 14 days of your 180-day no-water target: paper plates save the water that washing dishes takes. They cover the first 30 days; after that, wash dishes with the water you treat. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

1 adult at about 2,262 kcal a day and 1 person 65 or over at about 2,009 kcal a day: about 4,271 kcal a day × 14 days = 59,800 kcal. These are moderately active needs; the form does not ask sex, so men's and women's needs are averaged. Count calories, not servings. (Dietary Guidelines)

As everyday groceries: about $260 for 28 person-days (USDA Thrifty Food Plan, $8.44 a person a day, plus 10 % for a household of 2). Buy what you already eat, keep it in the pantry and use the oldest first. (USDA)

As bulk staples such as wheat, rice and beans: about $70 ($2.15 to $2.85 a person a day). Cheapest, but it needs cooking and is short on some vitamins, so it suits months rather than days. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU)

As freeze-dried or dehydrated meals: about $717 ($9 to $39 per 2,000 kcal, so $269 to $1,166). They need about 0.6 gallons of extra water a person a day to prepare. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)

A retail "30-day" food kit supplies about 1,290 to 1,730 kcal a day. For the average person here (about 2,135 kcal a day) one lasts about 18 to 24 days, not 30. Compare kits by total kcal. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices)

Dry food for the dog for 14 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog = 9.8 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the dog for 14 days (14 pet-days, at least a week): what it eats now, in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)

A way to cook without power, because your plan runs 14 days without a store, longer than food that needs no cooking comfortably covers: your gas range can boil water and cook while the gas still flows. If its igniter needs power, light a burner with a long match (check the manual first). Never use the oven or burners to heat the home. (Oregon OEM, CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

Fuel for a camp stove: about 0.2 lb of fuel a person a day × 2 people × 45 days = 18 lb, or 36 butane canisters of 0.5 lb each. Use it outdoors only, never indoors (carbon monoxide), and store it cool, away from heat. (CDC, Ready Reckoner research, EIA, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)
Toilet paper: about 1 roll a person every 5 days × 2 people × 14 days = 6 rolls. Better still, measure a week's use and double it for two weeks. (Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
Soap for 2 person-months: 2 people × 1 month. Each is 250 g of bathing soap and 200 g of laundry soap, about 900 g in all. (Sphere)

Period products for 2 cycles each, about 20 products a cycle (15 to 30). The form doesn't ask sex, so the plan counts half of the 1 person aged 13 to 64 who are not pregnant or nursing: 1 cycle's worth, about 20 products. Keep soap, clean underwear and pain relievers with them, and put used products in a separate bag. (CDC, Sphere, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

2 battery fans: 1 for the home plus 1 for the 1 person most at risk from heat (65 and over, babies, pregnancy). Fans help only while it is below 90 °F indoors; above that, go to a cooling centre. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
2 cooling towels, one for each person: wet them and wear them on the neck in a heat wave. (an estimate)
A heat plan: find your nearest cooling centre (dial 2-1-1), pick the coolest room, cover sunny windows, and agree who checks on whom. Never leave people or pets in a closed car. (CDC, Ready.gov)
1 room thermometer in the room where the most vulnerable person sleeps: fans help only while it is below 90 °F indoors, so when it reads higher, go somewhere cooler. (CDC)
2 warm blankets, one for each person: most homes already have them. (Ready.gov, Sphere)
2 sets of warm layers (coat, hat, gloves, dry socks), one for each person. (Ready.gov, CDC)

2 sleeping bags or extra heavy blankets, one for each person, rated for the coldest nights where you live: your cold target of 14 days is longer than the 3 days that blankets and warm layers cover. (Ready.gov, Sphere; some amounts are estimates)

A cold plan: pick one room to keep warm, close off the others, put towels under doors and cover windows at night, and find your nearest warming centre in case the home gets too cold. Never heat with a gas oven, grill, camp stove or generator indoors (carbon monoxide). People 65 and over should check the indoor temperature often. A body temperature below 95 °F needs medical help at once. (CDC, Ready.gov)

1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 30 days of it on hand. Your target is 180 days; beyond 30 days, ask your prescriber or insurer about a longer fill. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. For medicine the plan keeps at most a month on hand: agencies advise 7 days to two weeks (Red Cross, CDC, Florida), and a longer target is kept up with 60- to 90-day fills from your drug plan (Medicare). (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Healthcare Ready)

Your medication target is 180 days; the reserve at home covers the first 30 days. For the other 150 days, ask your drug plan whether it offers 60 to 90 day fills and which pharmacies give them, and refill as soon as the plan allows, so the supply at home stays ahead of each refill. (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Medicare)

1 person needs medicine kept cold, such as insulin. An insulated bag with fresh cold packs keeps it cool, never frozen, for about 1 day. Insulin in its vial or pen keeps working up to 28 days between 59 °F and 86 °F, so in a longer power cut keep it in the shade and below 86 °F; never use insulin that froze. Your power target is 90 days: plan a battery power station to run a small 12-volt cooler or the fridge (see its line), and a place with power you could go to. (FDA, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)
1 battery or hand-crank radio that gets NOAA Weather Radio, with a tone alert, for warnings when phones and power are down. (Ready.gov, NOAA)

Power banks: 2 phones × about 15 Wh a day (10 to 20) × 14 days without power = 420 Wh. Text instead of calling to save battery. Your power target is 90 days: past the first 14 days, recharge the power banks from the car or a solar panel (see the recharge line) instead of storing more. (Ready.gov, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

2 two-way radios for the 2 people aged 13 and over, to reach each other when phones are down. FRS radios need no licence; GMRS radios reach farther but need a $35 FCC licence that covers the family for 10 years. (FCC; some amounts are estimates)
2 written contact cards, one for each person aged 4 and over: an out-of-area contact, meeting places and key numbers. Phones die; paper does not. (Ready.gov)
1 paper map of your area, marked with meeting places and ways out. Save offline maps on your phone too. (Ready.gov)

Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $100, at least; half of 3 days of your usual spending ($1,900 a month) is less than that. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)

2 go-bags, one for each person: a sturdy bag you already own will do. Pack copies of documents on paper and on a flash drive, a phone charger, cash, a flashlight, a whistle, an old pair of prescription glasses, a change of clothes and sturdy shoes, and add water, food and medicines from your home supplies rather than buying them twice. You may get only minutes of warning (a local tsunami or a fast fire), so keep the bags packed by the door, and one at work if you work in a danger zone. Practise grabbing them and leaving. Plan where you would stay for about 5 days. (Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Water for the go-bags comes out of the water you store at home, not on top of it: the Red Cross three-day supply for leaving home, about 2 gallons a day for the 2 people × 3 days = 6 gallons. Keep it with the bags or take it as you leave. If you leave on foot, carry what you can (about 2.5 L each) and a filter; the rest goes in the car. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Food for the go-bags comes out of your home food supply, not on top of it: about 4,271 kcal a day × 3 days = 12,800 kcal of food that needs no cooking or refrigeration. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Dietary Guidelines)

1 pet carrier, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine it takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)
Water for the pet go-kit, set aside from your stored water rather than bought extra: 7 days for the dog = 2.2 gallons. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA, PetMD; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the pet go-kit, set aside from your pet food rather than bought extra: 10 days (7 to 10 days) for the dog = 10 pet-days. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA)
Keep the vehicle at least half full at all times, and fill up when leaving looks likely. (Ready.gov)

Person 1 travels 5 miles (8 km) by car to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 1.7 hours. Keep a get-home bag in the car: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Water for person 1's walk home: 1.7 hours × about 0.5 L an hour = 0.8 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. (FHWA; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 1's walk home: about 200 kcal for 1.7 hours on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)

1 car emergency kit: jumper cables or a charged jump pack you have tried, a flashlight, warm clothes, a blanket, bottled water and snacks, and your roadside-assistance number on paper; sand or cat litter in snow country. (Ready.gov)

1 family first-aid kit for 2 people: the Red Cross list for a family of 4 (bandages, gauze, tape, antiseptic wipes, gloves, a breathing barrier, a cold pack, tweezers, an emergency blanket and a thermometer). Add your own medicines and emergency numbers, and replace what you use. (Red Cross)

1 package of each of 4 kinds of non-prescription medicine (a pain reliever, an anti-diarrhea medicine, an antacid and an allergy medicine): one package of each lasts about 14 days for 4 people. That is 4 packages for 14 days. Follow the label, and ask a pharmacist about children's versions. (Ready.gov, CDC, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)
1 oral thermometer (non-mercury, non-glass; it is on the Red Cross kit list). (Red Cross)

Oral rehydration salts for vomiting, diarrhea or heat illness: 3 packets a person for every 2 weeks, at least 2 weeks' worth. For 2 people and 14 days that is 6 packets. Mix each packet into 1 litre of safe water. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
1 bleeding-control kit: a tourniquet and a pressure bandage for serious bleeding, and a Stop the Bleed class so you know how to use them. Serious bleeding can kill before help arrives. (DHS)

A wound-care and splint add-on for the first-aid kit: an irrigation syringe to wash a wound with clean water, wound-closure strips, an elastic wrap, a padded splint, trauma shears, blister dressings and gauze for packing a deep wound. Washing a wound out with plenty of clean water is the key step. Your plan runs past 14 days without a store, when a small wound has to be cared for at home. (Wilderness Medical Society, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)
A fire escape plan: two ways out of every room, a meeting spot outside, and a practice run with everyone. In a building, know both stairways and never use the elevator in a fire. (Ready.gov)

No smoke alarms yet: one on every level and in every bedroom, about 1 level and 1 bedroom for a home like yours = 2 alarms. Ask your fire department or the Red Cross first: some fire departments and the Red Cross install free smoke alarms. Buy them only if they cannot. Test them every month. (USFA, Ready.gov, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)

No carbon monoxide alarm yet: put one on every level where people sleep (1 for a home like yours), with battery backup. Replace them every 5 years or as the maker says. (CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

No fire extinguisher yet: 1 multipurpose (A-B-C) extinguisher for a home on one floor, kept near the kitchen. Learn how to use it before you need it. Small home fires are common: CPSC estimated about 6.6 a year for every 100 households, most of them cooking fires, and fire departments attend only about 3 in 100 of them. (USFA, CPSC; some amounts are estimates)

You live on floor 2, above the ground: 1 escape ladder for a bedroom window, in case fire or smoke blocks the way out, unless every bedroom already has a second way out such as a fire escape. Keep it by the window and practise with it. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Swap phone numbers with 2 neighbours and agree who checks on whom after a storm or an outage, when phones and roads may be down. (an estimate)

N95 respirators, for about 5 days of smoke, dust or ash: 1 a day for each of the 2 people aged 13 and over = 10 respirators. A well-fitting N95 protects far more than a cloth or surgical mask; replace it when breathing through it gets harder. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)

1 portable air cleaner with a HEPA filter for your clean room: for a room of about 200 square feet, a clean air delivery rate (CADR) of at least 130 for smoke (EPA's sizing, more for high ceilings). Keep a spare filter, and avoid air cleaners that make ozone. (EPA; some amounts are estimates)

Cheaper than an air cleaner: a 20-inch box fan with a 20 by 20 inch MERV 13 filter taped to its intake side, which EPA calls a cost-effective way to cut smoke indoors. Use a newer fan with safety features, and do not leave it running while no one is home. (EPA)

A clean-room plan for smoky or dusty days: pick one room with few windows and doors where everyone can sleep, keep it closed, set the heating or cooling to recirculate (or turn off fans that pull in outside air), run the air cleaner there, and do not fry food, burn candles or vacuum on those days. (EPA, CDC)

Savings goal: about 7 months of expenses ($13,300 at $1,900 a month), built up over time and kept apart from the supplies budget. You have about 0.5 months saved now. Planners often suggest 3 to 6 months; the CFPB says it depends on your situation. (FINRA, St. Louis Fed, CFPB)

Someone in your household earns money the others rely on: check whether your job offers disability insurance, and whether life insurance would carry the others through the years they would need. About 1 in 4 workers who start at 20 become disabled before retirement age. NAIC's buyer's guide helps you work out how much cover is enough. (SSA, NAIC)

Copy the 4 parts of FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit: IDs, financial and legal papers (including insurance), medical information, and household contacts. Keep copies in a waterproof, fire-resistant place or with someone you trust, with photos of your home and belongings, and update them once a year. (FEMA)
You have no condominium unit-owners insurance yet: get a quote and decide. Check what it pays if you have to live somewhere else for a while. (FEMA, Ready.gov, NAIC)

**For:** 1 adult and 1 older adult, with 1 dog  
**Where:** San Juan County, Puerto Rico (ZIP code 00907)  
**Home:** an owned apartment on floor 2, with city water, no heating and window air conditioning  
**Plan date:** October 1, 2026  
**Ready for:** very serious disruptions (the 1-in-100 setting), in today's climate. Water is planned at the basic level, about 1 gallon a person a day.[1]
> Ready Reckoner is an independent, open-source planning aid. It is not official emergency guidance, and not medical, legal or financial advice. Follow instructions from your local officials first.

**Where you are now:** getting started. **What is enough for your risks:** six months of supplies. At your budget, the bare minimum (three days of water, light, warmth and medicine) is in place by month 3 (January 2027), and everything by month 48 (October 2030). Start with the free steps under Your plan.
### The three things that matter most

1. Of 100 households like yours, about 45 (40–60) will have to leave home quickly at least once in the next 10 years. Know your evacuation zone and where you would go; leave when told.[2, 3] On the coast, strong shaking is the warning: walk to high ground as soon as it stops.[4]
2. Of 100 households like yours, nearly all (95 or more) will lose grid power for a day or more in the next 10 years. If you are not told to leave, be ready to manage about 3 months at home with no power, and about 6 months with no tap water.
3. Of 100 households like yours, about 65 (40–90) will be unable to shop for food and supplies for 3 days or more in the next 10 years. Keep about 2 weeks of food you normally eat, and 6 months of daily medicine on hand.

**What the plan assumes you already have:** a charged mobile phone, go-bag for each person, manual can opener, a cooking pot with a lid, three days of the food you normally eat and towels to wet and cool down. If any is missing, untick "Assume everyday basics" on the Have screen and the plan will add it.

### Leaving home

Warning can be as short as no warning at all (an earthquake) or as long as 3 days. For chemical spills and releases, plan for as little as a few minutes of warning; for tsunamis, 15 minutes. ### Staying in touch

**Four ways to reach each other.** Emergency planners call this a PACE plan: a primary way, an alternate, a contingency and an emergency way. Each one takes over when the one before it fails.[15] For a household it can be:

1. Primary: call.
2. Alternate: text. A text may get through when a call does not, and it saves battery.[16]
3. Contingency: everyone texts one out-of-state contact, who passes the news along.[16]
4. Emergency: go to the place you agreed to meet if you get separated.[16]

Planners group the needs a disaster makes harder under five headings, called CMIST: communication, maintaining health, independence, support and safety, and transportation.[141]

**Communication.** If speech, hearing or understanding is affected, carry cards that tell responders how to talk with you.[21] Ready.gov has guides in Spanish at listo.gov, and in 11 other languages.[142]

**Maintaining health.** Ask your doctor about an emergency supply of medicine, and plan backup power for equipment.[21] A power company's medical program may warn you of outages but does not promise faster repairs.[143]
**Independence.** Keep mobility aids, devices and service animals with you, so you stay independent.[141]

**Support and safety.** Make sure someone in your support network has a key to your home and knows how to use your equipment.[144] Many local emergency offices keep voluntary registries of people who may need help; your state's entry in this plan shows where to start.[21] Signing up does not guarantee help, so keep your own plan too.[145]
**Transportation.** Arrange accessible transportation ahead of time with your transit provider or emergency office.[21]
### Medicine

- 1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 30 days of it on hand. Your target is 180 days; beyond 30 days, ask your prescriber or insurer about a longer fill. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. For medicine the plan keeps at most a month on hand: agencies advise 7 days to two weeks (Red Cross, CDC, Florida), and a longer target is kept up with 60- to 90-day fills from your drug plan (Medicare).[9, 10, 13, 44, 45, 49, 50, 112, 147, 148, 171, 172, 173, 174]
- 1 person needs medicine kept cold, such as insulin. An insulated bag with fresh cold packs keeps it cool, never frozen, for about 1 day. Insulin in its vial or pen keeps working up to 28 days between 59 °F and 86 °F, so in a longer power cut keep it in the shade and below 86 °F; never use insulin that froze. Your power target is 90 days: plan a battery power station to run a small 12-volt cooler or the fridge (see its line), and a place with power you could go to. (some amounts are estimates)[9, 10, 12, 13, 87, 88, 89, 110, 133, 175]
### Antibiotics

- No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones.[23, 24, 176, 177]
### Older adults

- **Plan for older adults in the household.** Plan transport if help is needed to evacuate, copy Medicare and Medicaid cards, give someone in your support network a key and show them your equipment, and ask any clinic you rely on about its emergency plans (Ready.gov). Heat and cold are harder on people over 65, so set up daily check-ins in extreme weather.[104, 105, 144]
### Pets and animals

- Dry food for the dog for 14 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog = 9.8 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (some amounts are estimates)[9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 49, 50, 133, 178, 179, 180]
- 1 pet carrier, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine it takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time.[2, 178]
### Stress, mental health and the 988 line

**What helps.** Save 988 in every phone. It offers free, judgment-free support 24/7 for mental health, substance use and more, by call, text or chat.[181] After a disaster, the Disaster Distress Helpline offers crisis counseling 24/7 to anyone in emotional distress. Call or text 1-800-985-5990.[182] Write a short calm plan: what you might feel, what helps you, and who you will call.[183] Oregon's 2 Weeks Ready program even includes practicing mindfulness as a step in getting prepared.[184]

**What to avoid.** Do not keep the news on all day. No one, adult or child, benefits from graphic details or disturbing images.[185] Reach out before things feel unbearable. The 988 line supports people in emotional distress as well as in crisis.[181]
Pick a spot for each danger below, at home and at work, and practice going there.[5]
**Strong wind.** In a high wind or severe thunderstorm warning, go inside a sturdy building, to an inside room.[129] Stay away from windows while damaging wind is near.[130]
**Hurricane.** If officials tell your evacuation zone to leave, go right away. If you stay, use an inside room away from windows.[3]
**Earthquake.** Drop where you are, cover your head and neck, and hold on. Crawl under a sturdy table, or next to an inside wall away from windows. Do not run outside.[16]

**Chemical release.** If told to stay inside, go to an above-ground room with few openings. Close the windows, doors and vents, turn off fans and air conditioning, and seal the room with plastic sheeting and duct tape.[131]
**Radiation.** If officials warn of fallout, get inside, stay inside, stay tuned. Go to a basement or the middle of a brick or concrete building.[78]
Where to start in Puerto Rico, checked September 26, 2026:

- **Evacuation zones and registry:** No evacuation-zone lookup or registry for people who may need help in a disaster was found for all of Puerto Rico. Ask your municipio's emergency management office or the agency for all of Puerto Rico: Puerto Rico Emergency Management and Disaster Administration Bureau (https://manejodeemergencias.pr.gov/).
- **Alerts:** No alert sign-up was found for all of Puerto Rico. Emergency alerts still reach phones with no sign-up.[146]
- **Prescription refills:** No emergency refill rule was confirmed for Puerto Rico, which the 2022 review of states did not cover. Ask your pharmacist, and ask your drug plan about replacing lost medicine or a larger supply.[147, 148]
Keep paper copies in a waterproof pouch and photos you can reach from any phone. FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit groups them in four parts.[36]

- [ ] **Who you are:** photo IDs, birth certificates, Social Security cards, passports, and pet records.
- [ ] **Money and legal papers:** insurance policies, the lease or deed, a will and powers of attorney, bank and card contact numbers (not PINs), and recent tax returns.
- [ ] **Medical papers:** insurance cards, the written medicine list, prescriptions, and vaccination records.
- [ ] **Contacts:** family, doctors, the insurance agent, the landlord or lender, and employers.
### Decisions

- [ ] **Decide: ID for every person (passport book or card, or a state ID).** A passport book or card for each person, children included, proves who you are and your citizenship if other papers are lost, and the card shows no home address; get them before you need them. The federal fee schedule: a first adult book $165 and card $65 ($130 and $30 plus a $35 acceptance fee), for children under 16 a book $135 and card $50 (22 CFR 22.1).[36, 149, 150]
- [ ] **Decide: homeowners, condo or renters insurance.** You have no condominium unit-owners insurance yet: get a quote and decide. Check what it pays if you have to live somewhere else for a while.[36, 151, 152]
- [ ] **Decide: flood insurance, even outside a flood zone.** Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: about 3 in 10 flood insurance claims come from outside high-risk flood areas. A quote costs nothing, and a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings.[37, 151, 153, 154]
- [ ] **Decide: earthquake insurance.** A standard home policy does not cover earthquake damage. Decide whether earthquake insurance is worth its deductible where you live.[16]
- [ ] **Decide: disability and life insurance for the people who earn.** Someone in your household earns money the others rely on: check whether your job offers disability insurance, and whether life insurance would carry the others through the years they would need. About 1 in 4 workers who start at 20 become disabled before retirement age. NAIC's buyer's guide helps you work out how much cover is enough.[51, 155]
### Cash

- Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $100, at least; half of 3 days of your usual spending ($1,900 a month) is less than that. No agency gives a dollar amount. (some amounts are estimates)[9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 32, 36, 40, 133, 151]
### Savings

Of 100 households like yours, about 20 (10–35) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. The goal is about 7 months of expenses (about $13,300); you have 0.5 months saved. Your supplies plan is done by month 48. After that, your $50 a month for supplies could go here, reaching the goal in about 25 years from now. Three months of expenses, about $5,700, in about 12 years from now. This is a savings goal, kept separate from the supplies budget.
### If damage forces you out

If damage forced you out, 9 in 10 households like yours would be home again within about 9 months; living elsewhere that long costs about $5,200 at 30% of your monthly spending, which loss-of-use insurance pays for.[8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 29, 30, 32, 123]
What could reach a household like yours in San Juan County, Puerto Rico over the next 10 years: the likeliest events, and the rarer ones that can kill, most likely first.
### What to know and do
#### 1. Medical emergency
Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years.[17]
**Includes:** far from emergency care; falls.

**What helps.** Take a first-aid and bleeding-control class. You may be able to save a life by acting right after an injury, before help arrives.[18] If a teen or adult collapses and their heart stops, call 911 and push hard and fast in the center of the chest. This hands-only CPR needs no training. Note where the nearest heart defibrillator (AED) is; it talks you through each step.[19] Keep a stocked first-aid kit. Check it regularly and replace anything used or out of date.[20] Keep a list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies with your emergency supplies.[21] Know how to reach 911. Call if you can, and text where that service works.[22]
**What to avoid.** Do not start antibiotics on your own or take someone else's. The wrong medicine can delay the right treatment and cause serious side effects.[23] Do not use expired medicines.[24]
**How bad:** Serious (based on data).
#### 2. Hurricane
Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (88–98) will lose power or have damage from a hurricane or tropical storm in the next ten years.[9, 10, 11, 12, 13]
**Includes:** inland flooding from a tropical storm.

**What helps.** Know your evacuation zone, your routes and where you would stay. If you live in a mandatory evacuation zone and officials tell you to leave, go right away.[3] If you are not told to leave, shelter from the wind in a small inside room, closet or hallway away from windows, on the lowest floor that will not flood.[3, 25] Clear drains and gutters, bring in outdoor furniture, and think about storm shutters. Keep phones charged and have backup chargers.[3] A flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start, so buy it well before a storm.[26] If you would leave in an electric car, keep it fully charged all hurricane season.[27]

**What to avoid.** Never walk or drive through floodwater. One foot of moving water can sweep a car away.[26] Do not drive or charge an electric car that has been in floodwater. Salt water can start a battery fire.[27] Never run a generator inside your home or garage.[28]
**How bad:** Serious (mostly data).
#### 3. Burst pipe or water leak
Of 100 households like yours, about 14 will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.[29]
**Includes:** sewer backup.

**What helps.** Find your main water shut-off valve now, and show everyone how to turn it off. A burst pipe can flood a room quickly.[30, 31] Once a year, check the hoses to the water heater, washing machine, dishwasher and fridge, and replace any that crack or leak. A leak alarm can warn you early.[30] In freezing weather, let a faucet drip at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher.[31] Home and renters policies usually cover burst pipes. Many do not cover a sewer backup unless you add that cover, and floods need their own policy.[30]

**What to avoid.** Never thaw a frozen pipe with an open flame; use a hair dryer. Watch for electric shock around standing water.[31] Do not leave home while the washing machine or dishwasher is running.[30]
**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).
#### 4. Earthquake
Of 100 households like yours, about 9 will feel an earthquake strong enough to knock things off shelves in the next ten years.[32]
**Includes:** liquefaction; fire after an earthquake.

**What helps.** Practice Drop, Cover and Hold On: drop to your hands and knees, cover your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops.[16] Secure bookcases, water heaters, TVs and other heavy things, and keep heavy objects on low shelves. A standard homeowner's policy does not cover earthquake damage.[16] Store water in case the taps stop. Near a volcano, leave early if you are told to. Ash can travel hundreds of miles, so keep N95 masks.[33]
**What to avoid.** Do not run outside during shaking, and stay away from doorways.[16] Avoid driving in heavy ash.[33]
**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).
#### 5. House fire
Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (3–8) will have a house fire, in their home or next door in the next ten years.[13, 14]
**Includes:** carbon monoxide poisoning; lithium battery fire.

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside every bedroom and on every level, and test them each month.[34] Practice your escape plan twice a year, including finding your way out in the dark.[35] Sleep with bedroom doors closed. Teach children not to hide from firefighters.[35] If there is smoke, crawl low under it to your exit.[35] If you cannot get out, close the door, cover vents and cracks with cloth or tape, call 911, and signal from the window with a light-colored cloth or a flashlight.[35] Insurance and copies of your documents help you recover afterward.[36]

**What to avoid.** Before you open a door, feel the door and the knob. If either is hot, or smoke is coming around it, keep it closed and use your second way out.[35] If a person or pet is still inside, get out and tell firefighters right away.[35] If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll.[35]
**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).
#### 6. Volcanic eruption
Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (2–11) will have ash or mudflows from a volcano reach them in the next ten years.[9, 13]
**What helps.** The steps under "Earthquake" above apply here too.
**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).
#### 7. Flooding from rivers or heavy rain
Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (1–7) will be cut off or lose building services in a flood in the next ten years.[8, 9, 13]
**Includes:** flash flood; basement or street flooding in heavy rain.

**What helps.** Look up your address on FEMA's flood maps, and sign up for your community's warnings.[26] Homeowner's insurance does not cover flooding, and a flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start.[26] Renters can buy flood coverage for their belongings.[37] Know how you would get to higher ground or a higher floor.[26] A wildfire makes landslides more likely on a burned slope for several years. Near a burn scar, watch the forecast and listen for rushing water or a rumbling that grows louder.[38]

**What to avoid.** Six inches of moving water can knock you down, and one foot can sweep your car away.[26] Never drive around barriers on a flooded road. The road may have collapsed under the water.[39] Stay off bridges over fast-moving water.[26] Leave if you are told to, or if you feel unsafe near a slope.[38]
**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).
#### 8. Landslide
Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (1–10) will have a landslide cut off their road or damage their home in the next ten years. About 2 (1–7) in 1,000 will have one damage their home.[9, 13]
**What helps.** The steps under "Flooding from rivers or heavy rain" above apply here too.
**How bad:** Severe (rough data).
#### 9. Tsunami
Of 100 households like yours, about 1 (fewer than 1 to 2) will have to leave home or work for a tsunami warning in the next ten years.[9, 13]
**What helps.** The steps under "Earthquake" above apply here too.
**How bad:** Severe (rough data).
